newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal opposition dismisses early poll threat.
newsitem.headline: Portugal opposition dismisses early poll threat.

text.p: The leader of Portugal's main opposition party on Saturday dismissed government threats to call an early election, saying his Social Democrats would not provoke a political crisis that would keep Portugal from joining Europe's single currency.

Socialist Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said on Friday he wanted an early poll if the opposition pushed through local government spending plans that would either lead to tax rises or jeopardise Portugal's chances of joining the euro.
Centre-right Social Democratic Party (PSD) leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa said the government was overdramatising.
"The PSD will not create political instability now or at any time before 1999," Rebelo de Sousa told an international conference on Europe being held in Lisbon.
"We won't stir up a political crisis that would weaken Portugal's chances of being in the first group to join the euro," he told the conference.
He said the threat of early elections was a scare tactic.
"Antonio Guterres knows perfectly well that an early election would keep us out of the single currency."

Guterres' government was elected in October 1995 after pledging to lead Portugal into the single currency from the start in 1999 without raising taxes, but its victory fell four seats short of an absolute majority.

The government says that the opposition's proposals, which parliament approved in outline on Wednesday, would raise public spending by 150 billion escudos ($870 million). This would mean either a sharp increase in overall taxes or a widening of the budget deficit.
Reducing the budget deficit is a key condition for meeting the criteria for entry to European Economic and Monetary Union.
Jorge Coelho, assistant minister to the Prime Minister, said on Friday that the government would refuse to prepare the 1998 budget if the opposition parties did not withdraw their plans.
But Rebelo de Sousa said there was no incompatibility between the proposals and membership of the euro.
"There have been local spending laws in previous years and there will be one this year and there will be no crisis," he said.
